references.text: Lot chooses the land near the Jordan, which includes Sodom and Gomorrah, before the Lord destroys the cities.
The Lord tells Abraham about His plan to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah because of their great sin.
Moses reminds the children of Israel of the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of the Lord's wrath against sin.
The prophet Isaiah compares Israel's situation with Sodom and Gomorrah to emphasize the seriousness of their condition and the Lord's grace in allowing some to survive.
Isaiah prophesies that Babylon will become like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them, using the image of overturning directly.
Jeremiah prophesies an eternal destruction over Babylon, similar to what struck Sodom and Gomorrah.
Ezekiel mentions the sins of Sodom to warn Jerusalem about their own wickedness.
Amos uses God's overthrow (הפך) of Sodom and Gomorrah as a warning to Israel, with direct linguistic connection to Genesis 19:25.
Jesus warns that it will be better for Sodom than for the city that rejects the gospel messengers on the day of judgment.
Jesus uses the destruction of Sodom as an example of the sudden judgment that comes at the coming of the Son of Man.
Peter's second letter mentions God's punishment over Sodom and Gomorrah, which were reduced to ashes, as an example of judgment upon the ungodly.
Jude mentions Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities as examples of punishment with eternal fire for sexual immorality.
The Revelation of John uses an image of Sodom to describe the moral decay in a great city.
Direct allusion to Sodom as a symbol of open sin, which enriches the understanding of the city's fate.
